From eigenvalue \(\lambda _{i}\), derive effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\) and interpret \(\lambda _{i}<1\), =1, and >1 as decay, integration, and instability.
Find the fixed point under constant input and distinguish long memory near an integrator, a perfect integrator, and runaway positive feedback.

objectives: Draw the brain, body, and environment as a closed-loop dynamical system and distinguish feedforward commands, sensory feedback, state estimates, and external disturbances.
Generalize the first-order equation for one neuron to \(\tau dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\), correctly interpreting the direction of \(W_{ij}\) and every matrix shape.
When W is diagonalizable, transform population activity into its eigenbasis and derive mutually decoupled mode equations step by step.
From eigenvalue \(\lambda _{i}\), derive effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\) and interpret \(\lambda _{i}<1\), =1, and >1 as decay, integration, and instability.
Find the fixed point under constant input and distinguish long memory near an integrator, a perfect integrator, and runaway positive feedback.
prerequisiteBridge: First review scalar system \(\tau dh/dt=-h+u\). Without input, -h returns the state toward zero. Constant u shifts the fixed point to \(h^{*}=u\), and the solution decays as \(e^{-t/\tau }\). Feedback makes input depend on state, for example \(u=\lambda h+I\), changing the restoring coefficient from 1 to \(1-\lambda\). A recurrent population replaces scalar h by a vector and \(\lambda\) by matrix W; every eigenmode repeats the same scalar logic.

Fix the convention for W before calculation. Here \((Wh)_i=\sum _j W_{ij} h_{j}\), so \(W_{ij}\) is the effect of population j on population i: the column is source and the row is target. \(h\in \mathbb{R}^N\) is an N-unit activity column vector and \(W\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\). An eigenvector v satisfies \(Wv=\lambda v\), meaning a recurrent multiplication preserves the population pattern's direction and scales it by \(\lambda\).

Diagonalization \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\) requires N linearly independent eigenvectors. The columns of V are \(v_{i}\) and the diagonal entries of \(\Lambda\) are \(\lambda _{i}\). Writing \(h=V\alpha\) gives mode amplitudes \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), not another population of real neurons. An asymmetric W can have complex eigenvalues or be defective. Dynamics remain valid but require real oscillatory blocks, generalized eigenvectors, or the matrix exponential directly. The course first treats the diagonalizable case to expose timescale and stability clearly.

modules.title: Motor Control Is a Brain–Body–Environment Loop
paragraphs: Embed the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup.

A feedforward command acts in advance from a goal and internal model and can compensate for known delays, but it is vulnerable to unexpected disturbances and model error. A feedback controller corrects output using sensed state error and resists disturbances, but excessive gain combined with delay can oscillate. Biological control combines both, with spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum, basal ganglia, and motor cortex contributing on different timescales and representational levels rather than taking over sequentially.

A sensory signal is a delayed noisy observation, not the body's exact current state. A state estimate combines recent sensation, copies of motor commands, and a dynamics model to infer current latent position, velocity, and related variables. Feedback commonly computes error around this estimate. A central pattern generator (CPG) shows that a recurrent circuit can generate rhythmic motor output without an external command on every cycle; sensory feedback corrects phase and amplitude rather than generating each cycle from scratch.

A minimal scalar example writes body position dynamics as \(dx/dt=u+d\), with neural command u and external disturbance d. Proportional feedback \(u=-kx\) gives \(dx/dt=-kx+d\). Without persistent disturbance, x returns to zero at rate k. Under constant disturbance, fixed error is d/k. Raising k reduces steady error, but sensory delay, actuator limits, and noise constrain gain in real systems, foreshadowing recurrent-stability tradeoffs.

Distributed motor-cortical activity need not map one neuron to one muscle. A movement can be represented by a population trajectory: instantaneous activity is the dynamical state, and recurrent dynamics determine how the trajectory continues. The question expands from which neuron encodes which variable to which modes govern population-state evolution and which inputs alter initial conditions or the vector field. A linear network is not a complete motor theory, but it is the first decomposition of temporal structure.
keyPoints: Brain, body, and environment form a closed loop through commands, mechanics, disturbances, and sensory feedback.
Feedforward control anticipates; feedback corrects disturbances. Delay, noise, and gain set the stability costs.
A state estimate infers current latent state from delayed noisy observations, while a CPG demonstrates endogenous rhythm generation by recurrent dynamics.
Motor-population activity is a dynamical state; no mode should be assumed to equal one muscle or action variable.

derivation.title: How Proportional Feedback Rejects a Constant Disturbance
derivation.setup: Use normalized one-dimensional body dynamics \(dx/dt=u+d\) with target position 0 and proportional controller \(u=-kx\), where \(k>0\).

steps.title: Substitute the Feedback Law
steps.explanation: The controller converts positive position error into a negative command, yielding a first-order equation with constant forcing.

steps.title: Find the Fixed Point
steps.explanation: At steady state the derivative vanishes, so restoring command kx* balances disturbance d.

steps.title: Find Dynamics Relative to the Fixed Point
steps.explanation: Set \(e=x-x^{*}\). Constant terms cancel after substitution, and error decays as \(e^{-kt}\).

symbolNotes: k is feedback gain and has inverse-time units in this normalized equation.
d is written as a position-velocity disturbance. Mechanics with mass would change the units and state dimension.
derivation.unitsCheck: x has position units and \(dx/dt\), u, and d have position/time units. Thus kx has position/time units and k has units 1/time.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(k\to 0\), restoring feedback disappears and constant disturbance makes position drift. Increasing k reduces ideal-model error, but an unmodeled delay can destabilize high gain.

workedExample.title: Steady Position Error Under a Persistent Velocity Disturbance
workedExample.problem: For \(dx/dt=-2x+0.6\) and initial \(x(0)=1\), find the fixed point and time constant and compute position at \(t=1 \mathrm{s}\).
steps: Error \(e=x-0.3\) obeys \(de/dt=-2e\), so \(e(t)=0.7e^{-2t}\) and the time constant is 1/2 s.
workedExample.result: The system converges not to zero but to steady error 0.3; at 1 second its position is about 0.395.
workedExample.sanityCheck: At initial \(x=1\), derivative=\(-2+0.6=-1.4\), so the trajectory must move downward. The computed result has the correct direction.

pitfalls: Treating feedforward and feedback as mutually exclusive, although real actions commonly combine predictive commands with sensory correction.
Assigning one function to each motor region from a region list while ignoring circuits, parallel pathways, and the abstraction level of the course diagram.

modules.title: The Recurrent Population Equation and Eigenmode Decomposition
paragraphs: Begin with \(\tau dh/dt=-h+Wh+I\). Vector \(h\in \mathbb{R}^N\) contains the activities of N units, -h is unitwise leak, Wh is recurrent input, and I is external drive. Here \(W_{ij}\) points from j to i. In neuronal coordinates, each derivative depends on many \(h_{j}\) and the equations are coupled. We seek coordinates in which recurrent multiplication no longer mixes components.

Use right eigenvectors of W. If \(Wv_{i}=\lambda _{i} v_{i}\), multiplication by W rescales pattern \(v_{i}\) by \(\lambda _{i}\) without rotating it. Put these eigenvectors in the columns of V. If they are linearly independent, \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Expand activity as \(h=V\alpha\), where \(\alpha _{i}\) is the amplitude of population pattern i. This basis change leaves the physical state unchanged, just as a two-dimensional displacement can be expressed in oblique rather than x-y coordinates.

Substitute \(h=V\alpha\) into the original equation and take V to be time-independent: \(\tau V d\alpha /dt=-V\alpha +WV\alpha +I\). Using \(WV=V\Lambda\) and left-multiplying by \(V^{-1}\) gives \(\tau d\alpha /dt=-\alpha +\Lambda \alpha +V^{-1}I\). Since \(\Lambda\) is diagonal, row i contains only \(\alpha _{i}\): \(\tau d\alpha _{i}/dt=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). The complex network's linear dynamics decompose into familiar first-order systems.

The limitations matter. Eigenvectors of asymmetric W need not be orthogonal, so \(V^{-1}\) cannot be replaced casually by \(V^\mathrm{T}\). Nearly parallel eigenvectors make mode coordinates noise-sensitive. If W is defective, there is no complete ordinary eigenbasis; use Jordan form or \(e^{(-I+W)t/\tau }\) directly. The diagonalizable case highlights eigenvalue control of timescale but does not claim that cortical connectivity is symmetric.
keyPoints: The direction of \(W_{ij}\) follows by expanding \((Wh)_i\); here it is \(j\to i\).
\(h=V\alpha\) decomposes neuronal-coordinate activity into amplitudes of eigenvector patterns.
When W is diagonalizable, \(\Lambda\) does not mix modes and every \(\alpha _{i}\) follows an independent first-order equation.

derivation.title: From the Recurrent Equation to Decoupled Mode Equations
derivation.setup: Assume W has a complete eigenvector matrix V with \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Let \(h=V\alpha\) and define transformed input \(\widetilde I=V^{-1}I\).

steps.title: Substitute the Activity Expansion
steps.explanation: V is constant, so \(dh/dt=Vd\alpha /dt\). Replace each occurrence of h by \(V\alpha\).

steps.title: Use the Eigenvector Relation
steps.explanation: \(WV=V\Lambda\) because every column of V is an eigenvector of W.

steps.title: Left-Multiply by the Inverse Basis
steps.explanation: Left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\) removes V and projects external input into mode coordinates.

steps.title: Read the ith Diagonal Equation
steps.explanation: Only diagonal entry \(\lambda _{i}\) appears in row i of \(\Lambda\), so derivative i no longer contains another \(\alpha _{j}\).

symbolNotes: The columns of V are right eigenvectors; rows of \(V^{-1}\) read the coordinates \(\alpha\).
Ĩ_i is the input component in a left-eigenvector coordinate, not necessarily a simple Euclidean dot product.
derivation.unitsCheck: If V consists of dimensionless normalized patterns, \(\alpha\) and h have firing-rate units; W and \(\lambda\) are dimensionless, \(\tau\) has time units, and Ĩ has the same units as h.
derivation.limitCheck: For \(W=0\), choose \(V=I\) and \(\lambda _{i}=0\); every neuronal mode decays independently with \(\tau\). If W is already diagonal, the basis change leaves the coordinates unchanged.

workedExample.title: Common and Difference Modes in a Two-Neuron Network
workedExample.problem: Let \(W=[[0.8,0.1],[0.1,0.8]]\) and \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\). Find two normalized eigenvectors and eigenvalues and write the input-free mode equations.
steps: The mode equations are \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{+}/dt=-0.1\alpha _{+}\) and \(20 \mathrm{ms}\cdot d\alpha _{-}/dt=-0.3\alpha _{-}\). The common mode decays more slowly.
workedExample.result: Population activity decomposes into an aligned common mode with \(\lambda =0.9\) and an opposing difference mode with \(\lambda =0.7\).
workedExample.sanityCheck: Matrix \(\operatorname{trace} 1.6\) equals eigenvalue \(\operatorname{sum} 0.9+0.7\), and determinant 0.63 equals product \(0.9\times 0.7\).

pitfalls: Inferring source-target direction of \(W_{ij}\) by habit instead of expanding the matrix product.
Assuming every W has an orthonormal eigenbasis, a property restricted to special matrices such as real symmetric ones.

modules.title: Eigenvalues Control Timescale, Fixed Points, and Integration
paragraphs: Begin with input-free equation \(\tau d\alpha _{i}/dt=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}\). For real \(\lambda _{i}<1\), \(\alpha _{i}(t)=\alpha _{i}(0)\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})t/\tau ]\), giving \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda _{i})\). Positive recurrent feedback pushes \(\lambda\) toward 1, offsets leak, and lengthens memory; negative \(\lambda\) strengthens restoration and accelerates decay. Continuous-time stability requires Re(λ_i)<1, not \(|\lambda _{i}|<1\).

At \(\lambda _{i}=1\), restoring force vanishes. Without input \(\alpha _{i}\) holds its initial value; with time-varying input, \(\tau d\alpha _{i}/dt=\widetilde I_{i}(t)\), so the state accumulates the input integral—a perfect integrator. For \(\lambda _{i}\) slightly below 1 there is long but finite leakage; for \(\lambda _{i}>1\) small perturbations grow exponentially. Under constant input, algebraic fixed point \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\) may still exist, but it is unstable: any initial condition not exactly at that point departs. Nonlinear saturation may create another attractor, beyond the local range of this linear mode.

This also separates fixed point from timescale. For constant transformed input Ĩ_i and \(\lambda _{i}\ne 1\), \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\). The same small denominator creates both long \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and high steady-state gain, so near-integration amplifies constant bias and parameter error. Memory is the benefit and drift the risk. Negative feedback, multiple timescales, and nonlinear bounds can manage that sensitivity.

For arbitrary time-varying input, the mode response is the sum of decaying initial condition and input convolution. Kernel \(\exp[-(1-\lambda _{i})(t-s)/\tau ]/\tau\) weights only past input. As \(\lambda _{i}\) approaches 1, the kernel decays more slowly and older inputs continue to influence present state. The impulse response therefore exposes \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) directly, while transformed-input magnitude \(\widetilde I_{i}=V^{-1}I\) determines whether external drive enters that slow mode.

In population space, \(h(t)=V\alpha (t)\) sums all modal time courses. A slow mode may dominate the late trajectory even with a small initial projection because faster modes vanish first. An input's effect depends on which modes it projects onto, not only its total energy. An eigenvalue account of motor dynamics should report model fit, initial conditions, input projection, and observed timescale; a rotating trajectory alone does not identify an eigenmode as a behavioral command.
keyPoints: For a real eigenvalue \(\lambda <1\), \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1-\lambda )\); decay slows as the eigenvalue approaches 1.
\(\lambda =1\) removes leak and integrates input; \(\lambda >1\) makes the linear mode grow exponentially.
Approaching 1 increases both memory time and constant-input gain, amplifying bias and connectivity error as well.

derivation.title: Mode Solution, Effective Time Constant, and Fixed Point
derivation.setup: Consider one real mode \(\tau d\alpha /dt=-(1-\lambda )\alpha +\widetilde I\), initially with constant input.

steps.title: Find the Constant-Input Fixed Point
steps.explanation: Set the derivative to zero and solve for \(\alpha\)* when \(\lambda \ne 1\).

steps.title: Rewrite Error Relative to the Fixed Point
steps.explanation: Let \(e=\alpha -\alpha *\). Constant input and fixed-point terms cancel, leaving a homogeneous equation.

steps.title: Integrate the Homogeneous Equation
steps.explanation: Separate de/e from dt, integrate to obtain the exponential solution, and express its coefficient as an effective time constant.

steps.title: Extend to Time-Varying Input
steps.explanation: Use an integrating factor to retain the initial-condition term and weight transformed input at every past time s by the exponential impulse response. This convolution shows that a mode is a leaky temporal filter.

steps.title: Handle \(\lambda =1\) Separately
steps.explanation: The fixed-point formula containing \(1-\lambda\) cannot be used. The equation becomes derivative equal to input divided by \(\tau\).

symbolNotes: \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) is a positive decay time only for a stable real mode \(\lambda <1\). For \(\lambda >1\), use growth time \(\tau /(\lambda -1)\).
A complex \(\lambda\) produces oscillations set by its imaginary part, while 1-Re(λ) determines envelope stability.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\lambda\) is dimensionless, while \(\tau\) and \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) are times. \(\alpha\) and Ĩ share units, so \(\int \widetilde I ds/\tau\) retains the units of \(\alpha\).
derivation.limitCheck: \(\lambda =0\) gives \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau\). As λ→1^-, both \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and constant gain grow. For \(\lambda >1\), the exponent changes sign and the zero fixed point is unstable.

workedExample.title: Extending an Intrinsic 20 ms Time Constant to 1 s of Memory
workedExample.problem: A mode has \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\), \(\lambda =0.98\), initial amplitude 5, and no input. Find \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and amplitude after 1 s, then compare with \(\lambda =1\).
steps: After 1 s, \(\alpha =5e^{-1}\approx 1.84\). Recurrent feedback lengthens but does not eliminate decay.
For \(\lambda =1\) without input, \(d\alpha /dt=0\) and the amplitude remains 5 after 1 s. A persistent small bias would be integrated continuously.
workedExample.result: \(\lambda =0.98\) turns an intrinsic 20 ms constant into a 1 s leaky memory; only \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The incorrect formula \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=\tau /(1+\lambda )\) gives about 10 ms, the opposite of the memory-lengthening effect of positive feedback.

pitfalls: Applying the discrete-time condition \(|\lambda |<1\) directly to continuous-time equation \(\tau dh/dt=(-I+W)h\).
Continuing to use \(\alpha *=\widetilde I/(1-\lambda )\) at \(\lambda =1\), despite a perfect integrator having no finite fixed point under constant input.

figures.lectureTitle: Motor Systems and Linear Neural Dynamics
figures.title: In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes
figures.alt: A flow diagram that transforms population activity from neuronal coordinates through V inverse into mode amplitudes, evolves them independently in diagonal eigenvalue space, and reconstructs neuronal activity with V.
figures.caption: If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron.

synthesis: Motor control consists of closed-loop dynamics among brain, body, and environment, and neural activity is highly distributed. In a linear recurrent network, transforming individual neuronal activities into eigenmode coordinates decouples the system so each mode behaves like an independent first-order process. Eigenvalue \(\lambda\) sets effective time constant \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\): \(\lambda <1\) decays, \(\lambda \approx 1\) has long memory, \(\lambda =1\) is a perfect integrator, and \(\lambda >1\) grows without bound.
workedExamples: 【例题】题目：单元 time constant \(\tau =20 \mathrm{ms}\)，network eigenvalue \(\lambda =0.98\)。
Worked solution. \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}=20/(1-0.98)=1000 \mathrm{ms}=1 \mathrm{s}\)。recurrent feedback 把细胞尺度放大 50 倍。 Check. \(\lambda \) 是 dimensionless；\(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) 与 \(\tau \) 同单位。
【拓展例题】题目：快速 perturbation correction 与预先计划 ballistic movement。
Worked solution. 前者依 feedback/proprioception 与 brain-body loop；后者可含 feedforward command，但实际运动通常仍在闭环中。 Check. feedforward 不是"没有 sensory system"，而是在控制 law 中忽略/弱用实时反馈。

formulas.conditions: Exact cancellation of feedback and leak

glossary.definition: Control based mainly on a prior model or command rather than current feedback correction.
Online correction of action from sensory or state error.
Sensory feedback about body position or force.
A network with feedback loops among its units.
A population activity pattern associated with an eigenvector of W.
Conversion of the same state between neuronal and modal coordinates.
A mode's decay or integration timescale after feedback.
A state whose derivative is zero.
Whether a small perturbation returns to a fixed point.
A mode that accumulates input without leak.

commonTraps: Restricting a motor signal to one region and overlooking distributed population activity.
Confusing neuronal activity coordinates with eigenmode coordinates.
Treating an eigenmode as one neuron.
Writing \(V^{-1}WV=D\) without checking the convention that columns of V are right eigenvectors.
Using \(\tau /(1-\lambda )\) as a positive decay time when \(\lambda >1\).
Assuming \(\lambda =1\) is automatically robust, despite its sensitivity to perturbation.
Analyzing neural dynamics without body and environmental feedback.
Distinguish individual-neuron activity, population-mode coordinates, and behavioral state; do not turn an eigenmode into one “special neuron.”

questions.explanation: The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost. High gain amplifies noise and can cause overshoot or oscillation in a delayed loop, so stability must be assessed for the complete loop. Embed the motor system in coupled brain, body, and environment dynamics. Descending pathways change muscle activation; body mechanics convert activation into posture and velocity; gravity, contact, and object reaction forces alter body state; and proprioceptive, visual, and cutaneous signals return the outcome to the nervous system. Every arrow has delay and dynamics. Movement is therefore a time-evolving closed loop, not a static stimulus-response lookup.

choices.text: Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\).

The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty.

questions.explanation: Right eigenvectors of an asymmetric matrix are generally not orthogonal, so \(V^\mathrm{T}V\ne I\). The correct transform is \(\alpha =V^{-1}h\), equivalently using the associated left eigenvectors to read amplitudes. Use right eigenvectors of W. If \(Wv_{i}=\lambda _{i} v_{i}\), multiplication by W rescales pattern \(v_{i}\) by \(\lambda _{i}\) without rotating it. Put these eigenvectors in the columns of V. If they are linearly independent, \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\). Expand activity as \(h=V\alpha\), where \(\alpha _{i}\) is the amplitude of population pattern i. This basis change leaves the physical state unchanged, just as a two-dimensional displacement can be expressed in oblique rather than x-y coordinates.

questions.explanation: The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty. A tiny persistent bias, low-frequency noise, or connectivity error produces a much larger state displacement. This also separates fixed point from timescale. For constant transformed input Ĩ_i and \(\lambda _{i}\ne 1\), \(\alpha _{i}*=\widetilde I_{i}/(1-\lambda _{i})\). The same small denominator creates both long \(\tau _{\mathrm{eff}}\) and high steady-state gain, so near-integration amplifies constant bias and parameter error. Memory is the benefit and drift the risk. Negative feedback, multiple timescales, and nonlinear bounds can manage that sensitivity.

conceptTags: In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes
questions.stem: Which interpretation is supported by the schematic “In the Eigenbasis, Coupled Neuronal Dynamics Decompose into Independent Modes”?

choices.text: The ideal equation omits sensory delay, muscle dynamics, noise, saturation, and energetic cost.
The denominator \(1-\lambda\) shrinks from 0.02 to 0.001, multiplying timescale and constant-input gain by twenty.

A flow diagram that transforms population activity from neuronal coordinates through V inverse into mode amplitudes, evolves them independently in diagonal eigenvalue space, and reconstructs neuronal activity.
Inferring source-target direction of \(W_{ij}\) by habit instead of expanding the matrix product.

questions.explanation: If recurrent matrix W is diagonalizable as \(W=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), activity \(h=V\alpha\) expresses a neuronal-space pattern in eigenmode amplitudes. After left multiplication by \(V^{-1}\), each \(\alpha _{i}\) independently obeys \(\tau \dot{\alpha }_i=-(1-\lambda _{i})\alpha _{i}+\widetilde I_{i}\). Thus \(\lambda _{i}\), rather than one neuron, sets decay, integration, or growth of that population pattern. A basis change is a mathematical coordinate transformation; a mode is not an anatomical neuron.
